title: Eyelet lace scarf
subtitle: A simple two-row repeat of yarn-overs and K2tog for beginner lace.
excerpt: A flat scarf worked in a simple eyelet repeat of yarn-overs and K2tog decreases on 4 mm needles with DK yarn, finishing at 20 cm wide by 175 cm long. The two-row repeat is the simplest possible lace structure and a reliable first lace project.
sourceNotes: Simple eyelet patterns using alternating yarn-overs and knit-two-together are among the oldest knitting lace structures, documented in Weldon's Practical Knitter and Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870) for shawls and scarves.

content.text: This is a flat scarf worked from one short end to the other. It uses a simple eyelet repeat with alternating yarn-overs and K2tog decreases on 4 mm needles with DK yarn. It finishes at 20 cm wide and 175 cm long after blocking. The eyelet scarf is a good first lace project: there are only two different rows, and only one needs attention.

Flat construction was chosen because the two-row repeat is worked in rows. The pattern row uses (YO, K2tog) across: every yarn-over adds a stitch and the matching K2tog immediately removes one, so the stitch count stays constant. The wrong-side rows are all purl. The scarf uses about 175 g (395 m / 432 yards) of DK yarn. Blocking opens the eyelets significantly.
What you need

items.name: DK-weight wool or cotton yarn
items.substitutions: Wool blocks well. Cotton gives a stiffer, crisper eyelet. Avoid very hairy yarns that obscure the holes.

content.text: Gauge

22 sts x 30 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 4 mm needles. The eyelet fabric opens to approximately 20 sts per 10 cm after blocking. Each stitch off gauge changes the finished width by about 1 cm. Blocking can add 10 to 20 percent to both width and length; swatch in pattern and measure after blocking.
Stitches used
K (knit), P (purl), YO (yarn over), K2tog. On the RS row, work YO, K2tog alternately across the pattern section. On WS rows, purl across.
Pattern
Cast on
Cast on 44 stitches using the long-tail method: 2 garter border stitches each side and 40 pattern stitches (a multiple of 2). Tail length: (12.6 x 44) / 10 + 15 = about 70 cm.
Stitch count check-in: 44 stitches after the cast-on.
Body
Row 1 (RS): K2 (border), (YO, K2tog) 20 times, K2 (border). (44 sts)
Row 2 (WS): K2, P40, K2. (44 sts)

Repeat Rows 1 and 2 until the scarf measures 175 cm from the cast-on edge (blocked estimate). Work to approximately 155 cm off the needles to allow for blocking expansion. At the halfway mark (about 87 cm off the needles), count: still 44 stitches.
Cast off
Cast off on a WS row using the standard method. Work loosely.
Common faults

Holes appearing in the wrong places. On a WS row, a yarn-over from the previous RS row must be purled as a single stitch; if it is accidentally knitted together with the next stitch, it closes the eyelet. Purl each YO loop cleanly as one stitch on the WS rows.
Stitch count growing. On the RS row, each YO must be followed immediately by a K2tog. If a K2tog is missed, the YO remains as an extra stitch. Count before and after every RS row.
Eyelets barely visible. The scarf needs blocking; unblocked eyelet fabric looks compressed and flat.
Finishing
Weave in ends. Wet
blocking
is required: soak, press out moisture, and pin flat to the stated 20 x 175 cm. The eyelets open clearly after a thorough block.
Care
Handwash wool in cool water and lay flat to dry.
What to try next
The broken rib lace scarf combines a rib structure with periodic eyelet rows for a more complex texture. The feather and fan scarf uses a more elaborate pattern row.
